summary: Steel lookout on Kearsarge North (Pequawket), NH: reported built 1913, staffed until 1960, a 1948 construction helicopter crashed; Forest Service site open to hikers today.

facts.design: 28-foot steel tower with a standard NH wooden cab; enlarged cab built in 2000

access.note: The Forest Service runs the summit as a tower observation site reached on foot by two trails. Wikipedia says the tower is open to visitors to the summit.

visit.trail_note: Kearsarge North Trail is 3.1 miles from the parking lot on Hurricane Mtn Road in Bartlett; Weeks Brook Trail is 5.1 miles from South Chatham Road. The site has no restrooms and no potable water.

facts.agency: U.S. Forest Service, White Mountain National Forest (Saco Ranger District)

events.note: The Appalachian Mountain Club granted the state forestry commission use of the destroyed summit hotel for a fire lookout
Register and Wikipedia both date the tower to its 1913 start of service

Forest Service helicopter carrying 27,000 pounds of building materials for a summit tower reached the summit on December 5, 1948, then lost engine power about 20 feet up as the pilot was about to land and crashed; the pilot jumped clear. The sources do not say whether this replaced the 1913 tower.
Staffing by the state and the U.S. Forest Service ended
Saco Ranger District did some extensive repairs in late August and early September

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register and Wikipedia date the tower to 1913. Late-1948 newspaper reports describe materials flown up to build a tower on the summit. None of these sources says whether the 1948 work replaced the 1913 tower, so the story gives 1913 as the register's date and reports the 1948 work as it stands.
The register gives the tower site as 3,194 ft (974 m). Wikipedia and the 1948 article give the mountain summit as 3,268 ft (996 m). The record's 973.5 m matches the register's tower-site figure.

notes_for_editor: Current staffing is unconfirmed. The 2025 chapter report says Kearsarge was staffed, but Wikipedia says that name also belongs to a Merrimack County mountain, so the report cannot be tied to this tower. The NHLR entry gives no visit reports. The 28-foot height is read as the tower's height from the register's '28' steel tower' line. The 2025 Press Herald and SectionHiker results were not opened, so 'open to the public' rests on the Forest Service page and Wikipedia. climbable=true follows the observation-site description and the 'fire tower' visit wording; check before publishing.
